title: Uniform strict polygon gap for integral codegrees
statement:
Work in the real field $\mathbf R$ (a field in the sense of [def-weil-field]) with its usual order. Fix integers $N\geq3$ and $d\geq1$. There is a real number $\eta(N,d)>0$ such that the following holds for every tuple of integers $e=(e_0,\ldots,e_{N-1})$ satisfying
$$e_0=0,\quad e_{N-1}=d,\quad 0\leq e_i\leq d\ (0\leq i\leq N-1),\quad e_i<\frac{di}{N-1}\ (0<i<N-1).$$
For every tuple of real weights $w_0\geq\cdots\geq w_{N-1}=0$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}w_i=1$, put
$$B(e,w)=\min_{0=i_0<i_1<\cdots<i_h=N-1}\ \sum_{j=0}^{h-1}(e_{i_j}+e_{i_{j+1}})(w_{i_j}-w_{i_{j+1}}).$$
The minimum is over all increasing subsequences containing both endpoints. Then
$$B(e,w)\leq\frac{2d}{N}-\eta(N,d).$$
The number $\eta(N,d)$ is uniform over the finitely many admissible integer tuples $e$.

proof.text: Put $n=N-1\geq2$, $\alpha=d/n>0$, $\delta=1/n$ and $\eta=\delta/(Nn)=1/(Nn^2)>0$. Fix admissible $e,w$. Set $D_i=\alpha i-e_i$. Then $D_0=D_n=0$ and, for $0<i<n$, $di-ne_i$ is a positive integer, so $D_i\geq1/n=\delta$. Since $0\leq w_i\leq w_0$ and $w_n=0$, normalization gives $1\leq n w_0$, hence $w_0\geq1/n$. For an endpoint-containing subsequence $I=(a_0,\ldots,a_h)$, write $C_e(I)$ for its cost in the statement and $C_\alpha(I)$ for the same cost with $e_i$ replaced by $\alpha i$. There are finitely many such subsequences and at least one, so $B(e,w)\leq C_e(I)$ for each one.

source.place: Lemma 6, corrected polygon estimate; quantitative strict refinement by the worker

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-finite-convex-minorant-chain] to the decreasing sequence $w_0,\ldots,w_n$. It supplies an endpoint-containing subsequence $I=(a_0,\ldots,a_h)$ and its affine interpolant $v_i\leq w_i$, with nondecreasing adjacent differences. Write $S=\sum_{i=0}^n v_i$. In particular $v_0=w_0$, $v_n=0$, and $S\leq\sum_iw_i=1$.

source.place: Lemma 6 and Figure 2: choose a lower convex contact chain

proof.text: The adjacent differences supplied by [lem-sfb-finite-convex-minorant-chain] are nondecreasing. For $0<i<n$, each of the first $i$ differences is at most each of the last $n-i$ differences. Summing over these pairs gives $(n-i)(v_i-v_0)\leq i(v_n-v_i)$, hence $v_i\leq(1-i/n)w_0$. The endpoint cases are equalities. Summing gives $S\leq Nw_0/2$, or $w_0\geq2S/N$.

source.place: Lemma 6: the chord inequality for the finite convex interpolant

proof.text:
For each consecutive pair $p<q$ in $I$, affine interpolation gives $\sum_{i=p}^{q-1}(v_i+v_{i+1})=(q-p)(w_p+w_q)$. Also $(p+q)(w_p-w_q)-(q-p)(w_p+w_q)=2p w_p-2q w_q$. Summing the latter identity over $I$ telescopes to zero, since the endpoints are $0$ and $n$ and $w_n=0$. Therefore
$$C_\alpha(I)=\alpha\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(v_i+v_{i+1})=\alpha(2S-w_0)\leq\frac{2\alpha n}{N}S\leq\frac{2d}{N}.$$
The first inequality uses Step 3; the second uses $S\leq1$ and $\alpha n>0$. This derives the corrected factor-two bound directly.

source.place: Lemma 6, corrected polygon estimate; quantitative strict refinement by the worker

proof.text:
First suppose $h\geq2$, so $I$ has an interior vertex. Each edge of $I$ then has at least one interior endpoint. Thus $D_{a_j}+D_{a_{j+1}}\geq\delta$ for every edge. All weight differences are nonnegative, so
$$C_\alpha(I)-C_e(I)=\sum_j(D_{a_j}+D_{a_{j+1}})(w_{a_j}-w_{a_{j+1}})\geq\delta\sum_j(w_{a_j}-w_{a_{j+1}})=\delta w_0\geq\delta/n.$$
Combining with Step 4 and $\eta\leq\delta/n$ gives $B(e,w)\leq2d/N-\eta$ in this case.

source.place: Lemma 6, corrected polygon estimate; quantitative strict refinement by the worker

proof.text: It remains to treat $h=1$, so $I=(0,n)$ and $v_i=(1-i/n)w_0$. Here $Nw_0/2=S\leq1$, so set $s=2/N-w_0\geq0$. The endpoint-only cost is $C_e(0,n)=d w_0=2d/N-ds$. If $s\geq\delta/(dNn)$, this cost is at most $2d/N-\delta/(Nn)=2d/N-\eta$, proving the claim. Hence only $0\leq s<\delta/(dNn)$ remains.

source.place: Lemma 6, corrected polygon estimate; quantitative strict refinement by the worker

proof.text:
For $1\leq k\leq n-1$ put $A_k=d w_k-\alpha(n-k)w_0$. Since $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}w_k=1-w_0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)=n(n-1)/2$, direct summation gives
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}A_k=d(1-Nw_0/2)=dNs/2.$$
There are $n-1>0$ summands, so some $k$ satisfies $A_k\leq dNs/(2(n-1))$: otherwise summing the $n-1$ strict reverse inequalities contradicts the displayed identity. Fix such an interior $k$.

source.place: Lemma 6, corrected polygon estimate; quantitative strict refinement by the worker

proof.text:
Insert this $k$ between the endpoints. Expanding its cost and using $e_k=\alpha k-D_k$ gives
$$C_e(0,k,n)=e_k(w_0-w_k)+(e_k+d)w_k=e_k w_0+d w_k=d w_0+A_k-D_k w_0.$$
Using $D_k\geq\delta$, $w_0\geq1/n$, $d w_0\leq2d/N$, and Step 7, we obtain
$$C_e(0,k,n)\leq\frac{2d}{N}+\frac{dNs}{2(n-1)}-\frac{\delta}{n}<\frac{2d}{N}+\frac{\delta}{2n(n-1)}-\frac{\delta}{n}\leq\frac{2d}{N}-\frac{\delta}{2n}\leq\frac{2d}{N}-\eta.$$
Here the strict inequality uses $s<\delta/(dNn)$; the next uses $n\geq2$, and the last uses $N\geq3$. Since $B(e,w)\leq C_e(0,k,n)$, this finishes the remaining case. The single positive choice $\eta(N,d)=1/(N(N-1)^2)$ works for every admissible integral tuple, so it is uniform as required.
